subject: english-language
title: Sound and Exaggeration
welcome_lead: Alliteration and onomatopoeia tickle the ear; hyperbole goes huge.
meta_desc: KS3 English Language adventure on alliteration, onomatopoeia and hyperbole.
final_note: You can now spot sound devices and exaggeration with confidence.

walkthroughs.body_html: 'Silent, slithering snakes' uses alliteration — the repeated 's' also creates sibilance (hissing).
Onomatopoeia: 'crash', 'sizzle', 'buzz'. Words that sound like what they describe — powerful in poetry and comics.
'I could eat a horse' isn't lying — it's hyperbole, a clear exaggeration to communicate strong feeling.

Why does English vocabulary have so many synonyms?
options: Layered historical contact — Old English, Old Norse, Norman French and Latin — left English with multiple words from different sources for similar concepts (e.g. ask/question/interrogate).
Because English speakers have always wanted to make things complicated.
English has many synonyms because Shakespeare invented lots of words.
Convergence means two languages merge into one new language.
A morpheme is a sound that has no meaning.
The smallest unit of meaning in a language — a word like 'unhappiness' has three morphemes: un-, happy, and -ness.

mcqs.q: What is convergence in accommodation theory?
options: When a speaker adjusts their speech to be more similar to their interlocutor's — to express solidarity, gain approval or ease communication.
Convergence is when two speakers start using identical accents permanently.
